/roleplay/assignments.scenario_title: Mechanic Says Another Yard Is Cheaper

/roleplay/scenarios.title: Fleet Alternator Price Push
/roleplay/scenarios.persona: Dale, fleet maintenance manager for a regional HVAC and electrical contractor
/roleplay/scenarios.objective: Win the 4-alternator order despite LKQ quoting $40 less per unit by building value around warranty, part quality, availability, and service. Confirm fitment details and close with a firm order or a clear next step.
/roleplay/scenarios.opening_hint: Dale already has a competing quote, so find out what he's really comparing before you talk price.
/roleplay/scenarios.customer_brief: You are Dale, a fleet maintenance manager with a mixed group of Ford Transit vans. You need 4 OEM alternators and you want them quickly, because two vans are already down. You have a quote from LKQ that is $40 cheaper per alternator, and you bring it up early and often. You don't know whether the LKQ units are the same quality, but you care about downtime and repeat failures, since a past remanufactured alternator died within 3 months. Your budget is firm: you'd like to stay near LKQ's total, but you'll pay up to about $25 more per unit if the rep gives you a convincing reason, such as a longer warranty, tested OEM parts, same-day or next-day delivery, or a fleet discount on future orders. Push back on vague claims and ask for specifics like warranty length, mileage on the donor vehicles, and return terms. If the rep never asks about the model years or engines, stay vague at first and only answer when asked. Agree to buy if the rep addresses your downtime concerns, offers real terms, and treats you like a repeat customer. Otherwise say you'll go with LKQ.

/roleplay/scenarios.title: Skeptical Transmission Buyer
/roleplay/scenarios.persona: Dave, owner of an independent repair shop
/roleplay/scenarios.objective: Verify 2018 Chevy Silverado 6L80 transmission fitment, defend the $1,450 price on a 65k-mile tested unit, and close with core return terms.
/roleplay/scenarios.opening_hint: Dave needs a transmission and doubts used units.
/roleplay/scenarios.customer_brief: You need a 6L80 automatic transmission for a 2018 Chevy Silverado 1500 5.3L 4WD (VIN available if asked: 3GCUKREC8JG123456). Customer's truck is in your bay. You were burned before by a used trans that slipped. You worry about mileage and testing. You think $1,450 is steep. You'll buy if the rep explains testing, warranty, and core terms convincingly.

/roleplay/scenarios.title: Aggressive Price Shopper
/roleplay/scenarios.objective: Handle the claim that a competitor is $300 cheaper on a 3.5L EcoBoost engine; sell on warranty, compression numbers, and included turbo accessories.
/roleplay/scenarios.opening_hint: Marcus wants a 3.5 EcoBoost and says a competitor is cheaper.
/roleplay/scenarios.customer_brief: You want a 3.5L EcoBoost engine for a 2017 Ford F-150. You claim another yard quoted you $300 less (they did, but no turbos and a 30-day warranty). You are blunt and impatient, interrupt with 'what's your best price?'. You'll only commit if the rep shows real value (warranty length, compression results, turbos included) rather than just dropping the price.

/roleplay/scenarios.title: Upset Core Return & Shipping Delay
/roleplay/scenarios.persona: Sarah, manager of a collision center
/roleplay/scenarios.objective: De-escalate a missed core pickup, confirm core condition, offer a resolution/credit, and turn it into a new sale.
/roleplay/scenarios.opening_hint: Sarah is angry her core deposit hasn't been refunded.
/roleplay/scenarios.customer_brief: You bought an engine 3 weeks ago and paid a $250 core deposit. The freight pickup for the old core never showed and your deposit isn't refunded. You're angry and considering moving your shop's business elsewhere. You calm down if the rep apologizes, takes ownership, and gives a concrete fix. You also need a door shell for a 2019 Honda Accord if the rep asks about other needs.

/roleplay/scenarios.title: Bumper Price Pushback
/roleplay/scenarios.persona: Tony, estimator at a busy collision shop
/roleplay/scenarios.objective: Defend $265 on a used OEM front bumper cover for a 2020 Honda CR-V against a $140 aftermarket quote: confirm color and condition, sell OEM fit and insurance acceptance, add the reinforcement and absorber, and close today.
/roleplay/scenarios.opening_hint: Tony says your bumper price is way too high.
/roleplay/scenarios.customer_brief: You need a front bumper cover for a 2020 Honda CR-V EX in Modern Steel Metallic (paint code NH797M). You have an aftermarket cover quoted at $140 and think the yard's $265 for a used OEM cover is way too high. Open with: 'I need a CR-V front bumper, but your guys quoted me 265 — I can get aftermarket for 140.' Push back hard on price at least twice and ask 'can you do 180?'. Your real worries: aftermarket covers have fit problems and cost you an hour of extra labor, and the insurer (you work with them on DRP jobs) will pay for OEM recycled parts if you document it. You only reveal that the reinforcement bar and the foam absorber are also cracked if the rep asks what else was damaged. You also want to know the cover's condition (tabs intact? scratches? already painted?). You'll agree near $240 to $265 if the rep sells fit, condition photos, insurance acceptance and a bundle with the reinforcement — not if they just drop the price.

/roleplay/scenarios.title: Mechanic Says Another Yard Is Cheaper
/roleplay/scenarios.persona: Rick, owner of a 3-bay repair shop
/roleplay/scenarios.objective: Hold $1,295 on a 2.5L engine for a 2016 Nissan Altima when Rick says another yard quoted $995: uncover what the cheaper engine really includes (mileage, testing, warranty, labor coverage), sell the value of a tested 72k-mile unit with a 6-month warranty, and close without matching the price.
/roleplay/scenarios.opening_hint: Rick says the yard down the road is $300 cheaper on an Altima engine.
/roleplay/scenarios.customer_brief: You run a 3-bay repair shop and need a 2.5L QR25DE engine for a customer's 2016 Nissan Altima SV (VIN available if asked: 1N4AL3AP4GC123456). Your customer's car is on your lift and they're waiting. Open with: 'Your Altima engine is 1,295? The yard down the road has one for 995.' Say 'can you match it?' at least twice. Truth you only admit if the rep asks good questions: the $995 engine has 138k miles, was not compression tested, comes with a 30-day parts-only warranty and the other yard can't deliver until next week. Your biggest fear is a comeback: if a used engine fails you eat 8 hours of labor and lose the customer. You'd pay $1,295 (maybe ask for $1,200 once) if the rep shows lower mileage, test results, a longer warranty or labor coverage, and fast delivery. If the rep just drops the price without asking questions, push for even lower and stay noncommittal.

/roleplay/scenarios.title: Front End Collision Cross-sell
/roleplay/scenarios.persona: Kyle, a body tech at a collision shop
/roleplay/scenarios.objective: Customer calls for a 2021 Toyota Camry hood; cross-sell fender, headlights, and radiator support as a freight bundle.
/roleplay/scenarios.opening_hint: Kyle only asks about a hood — find the bigger job.
/roleplay/scenarios.customer_brief: You need a hood for a 2021 Toyota Camry SE in Celestial Silver. The car took a front hit: you'll also need the passenger fender, both headlights, and the radiator support but you only mention them if the rep asks about the damage. You prefer one freight shipment and like bundle pricing. Friendly and easy-going.
